title: A Grip That Signals Both Ways

scenes.tts: When a receptor grips a ligand that is stuck to another cell, which cell gets the message? The receptor sits in the upper cell. Its ligand is held in the membrane of the lower cell. Does the message reach one of them, or both? Often, both.
scenes.visual: Two cells, one above the other, a gap between them. The receptor hangs from the upper cell, its ligand rises from the lower. The cells close, the receptor's cup grips the ligand's knob, and a question mark appears in each cell. Both pulse at the answer.
scenes.narration: When a receptor grips a ligand that is stuck to another cell, which cell gets the message? The receptor sits in the upper cell. Its ligand is held in the membrane of the lower cell. Does the message reach one of them, or both? Often, both.

scenes.tts: Many ligands are made as membrane proteins. Such a ligand can have a tail inside its own cell. A tail in the cytosol is what you expect of a receptor. When the two proteins bind, the receptor signals into its own cell. That is the forward signal. A second message passes into the cell that carries the ligand. That is reverse signaling.
scenes.visual: The ligand grows a tail into its own cell, matching the receptor's inner tail. The grip closes again: a green pulse runs up the receptor and out into the upper cell (forward signal), then an orange pulse runs down the ligand's new tail and out into the lower cell (reverse signal).
scenes.narration: Many ligands are made as membrane proteins. Such a ligand can have a tail inside its own cell. A tail in the cytosol is what you expect of a receptor. scenes.tts: Ephrins are the clearest case of reverse signaling. A B type ephrin crosses the membrane once and ends in a short tail. The tail contains no enzyme. Yet when the ephrin meets the outer part of its receptor, its tail gains a phosphate on a tyrosine. That outer part has no kinase, and neither does the ephrin. So a kinase in the ephrin's own cell must do the work.

scenes.visual: Zoom to the ligand's cell. The upper cell falls away, leaving only the receptor's outer part gripping the ephrin. The tail shows an empty dashed slot, then a phosphate lands on a tyrosine dot. Two crossed-out kinase chips (one by the receptor fragment, one by the ephrin) and a dashed purple question-mark kinase inside the ephrin's cell.

scenes.tts: Which kinase? Sark family kinases gather where B type ephrins cluster, and they help to put phosphate on the tail. An adaptor then binds the phosphorylated tyrosines. It connects the ephrin to proteins that reshape the actin skeleton. This is one route; P D Z proteins offer another.
scenes.caption: Which kinase? Src-family kinases gather where B-type ephrins cluster, and they help to put phosphate on the tail. An adaptor then binds the phosphorylated tyrosines. It connects the ephrin to proteins that reshape the actin skeleton. This is one route; PDZ proteins offer another.
scenes.visual: The question-mark kinase becomes a purple Src blob and slides against the tail; a second ephrin joins to make a cluster and a second Src blob joins it. Phosphates fly from each Src onto the tails. An adaptor chip binds the phosphates and an orange arrow carries on to an actin chip.

scenes.tts: Suppose you delete the gene for a B type ephrin, and an organ fails to form. You have removed the forward signal, the reverse signal, and the grip that held the cells together. The knockout cannot tell you which loss caused the defect. So change the ephrin instead. Keep its outer part and its membrane segment, and remove only the tail. Check that it reaches the surface, then measure the forward signal. Reverse signaling through the tail is gone.

scenes.visual: Zoom out to both cells. The ephrins vanish; the forward signal, the reverse signal and the grip each get a red cross. The ephrins return, then their tails drop away. The grips close; a green pulse runs up and out, an orange pulse runs down the tail-less ephrin and stops, its arrow crossed out.

scenes.tts: Other ligands work this way too. Membrane bound T N F acts as a receptor, and so does a fly semaphorin. In each pair, the protein named receptor also gives a signal. The protein named ligand also receives one. The names were fixed by history. So keep this rule: a membrane ligand can receive a signal as well as give one.

scenes.visual: The two-cell picture with tails restored. The lower label changes from ephrin to TNF to semaphorin while both signals run, green up and orange down. The labels receptor and ligand swap places. Both arrows stay lit.
